subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Dear Amandeep, I am still shaking from this morning. Near the station a man collapsed on the pavement, and about thirty of us were walking past. I slowed down and looked at everyone else. Nobody stopped, so I thought maybe it is not serious, maybe he is drunk, maybe someone has already called. Then I saw his hand twitch and felt sick. I called out, "You, in the blue jacket, call an ambulance!" and the man in the blue jacket froze, then dialled. A woman knelt beside the collapsed man. An ambulance came within minutes. I do not know what happened to him afterwards. But I know how close I came to walking on. — Noor

qa.q: About how many people were walking past the man who collapsed?
qa.a: About thirty people were walking past.

qa.q: Why did Noor think it might not be serious when nobody stopped?
qa.a: Noor read the crowd's inaction as a sign it was not serious, each person taking the others' calm as proof; the twitching hand broke that belief and brought a sick feeling.

qa.q: What turning point led Noor to act?
qa.a: Noor saw the man's hand twitch, felt sick, and called out to one person in a blue jacket to phone an ambulance instead of waiting.

qa.q: What might the man in the blue jacket have been feeling when Noor called out?
qa.a: The man in the blue jacket probably felt startled and suddenly responsible; being named pulled him out of the crowd's passive waiting, and he dialled.

grounding: A commuter sees someone collapse while the crowd keeps walking, each reading the others' inaction as proof it is not serious.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Simran, listen, it's Jasleen, and I need to say what I saw. Last night on the market road a man kept following a woman and shouting things at her, and there were maybe twenty people around: the tea stall, two rickshaw drivers, some couples. Everyone kept walking, and so did I. All those calm faces made me think it was not serious. She was gripping her bag and walking faster. I turned around after twenty steps, walked up to the tea vendor and said loudly, "Please call the police helpline." Then the two rickshaw drivers stood near her. The man slunk off. I am shaking even now.

qa.q: How many people were around when the man followed the woman?
qa.a: There were maybe twenty people around.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen keep walking even though the woman was gripping her bag?
qa.a: Jasleen took the calm faces of the crowd as proof it was not serious, an assumption shared by everyone; afterwards the shaking shows how uneasy that decision felt.

qa.q: What choice made Jasleen turn around after twenty steps, and what did that action achieve?
qa.a: Jasleen turned back, spoke loudly to the tea vendor to call the police helpline, and this drew the rickshaw drivers to stand near the woman until the man left.

qa.q: What might the woman have been feeling while everyone walked past?
qa.a: The woman was probably frightened and alone, gripping her bag and walking faster while the crowd's silence gave her no sign anyone would help.

grounding: A commuter sees a woman harassed while the crowd keeps walking, and pluralistic ignorance makes each person read others' inaction as proof it is not serious.
